strengths: The paper addresses a compelling computational-imaging problem: recovering 31 spectral channels from a single filterless measurement with the same spatial pixel count. The combination of patchwise conditional diffusion, global optical consistency, and least-squares patch rescaling is a useful contribution under Algorithms/General.

The main simulation results are strong. On ARAD1K, Table 1 reports 34.63 dB PSNR versus 31.77 dB for the strongest evaluated baseline, with corresponding improvements in SAM and SSIM. Eight existing reconstruction methods are retrained for the proposed measurement model.

The ablations substantiate the importance of guidance and rescaling. Table 2 shows that guidance improves 64-pixel patch reconstruction from 32.16 to 34.67 dB, with an even larger benefit for 32-pixel patches. The optical-design comparison also demonstrates a substantial advantage over uncoded grayscale measurements.

The evaluation extends beyond the main benchmark through high-resolution cross-dataset examples, a noise-training study, and uncertainty maps whose reported correlation with error is promising. The supplement provides useful architecture and optical-simulation details.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not isolate the claimed advantage of patch-based modeling over full-field reconstruction. A matched full-field conditional diffusion baseline and a patchwise deterministic model with comparable optical consistency would help separate the effects of patch training, diffusion priors, model capacity, and iterative guidance. Existing guidance and patch-diffusion components are acknowledged, so this distinction matters for assessing the methodological advance.

The abstract's claim that local optical cues are sufficient to capture full spectral information is stronger than the evidence supports. The forward operator is highly underdetermined; spatially uniform regions, for example, provide only a weighted spectral sum away from boundaries. Successful reconstruction therefore depends on learned scene priors. Tests on ambiguous spectra or unfamiliar materials would better establish when the method recovers spectral evidence versus predicts plausible spectra.

All measurements are simulated using a known, shift-invariant PSF. The Gaussian-noise experiment is useful, but sensitivity to PSF calibration errors, field-dependent aberrations, and fabrication mismatch remains untested. A hardware prototype is not essential for this algorithmic contribution, but practical camera and field-of-view claims should remain conditional on these assumptions.

High-resolution generalization is evaluated on only 10 scenes each from ICVL and Harvard and five CAVE scenes, without a stated selection protocol or cross-dataset baseline comparisons. Spectral-angle results, uncertainty calibration, and measured high-resolution runtime/memory are missing. Table 4 already reports approximately 22 seconds per 256 × 256 reconstruction at the default guidance setting, before repeating sampling for uncertainty.

Table 1 and the main text label the RGB experiments as Bayer measurements, whereas Supplement Section 11 states that they use three full-resolution filtered channels, effectively three sequential captures. This materially changes the acquisition model. The claimed small drop for a true Bayer mosaic should be quantified, and the existing results should be relabeled.

Several reproducibility details need clarification: the guidance step size is unspecified, Algorithm 1 omits the gradient normalization in Equation 6, and the main-text squared noise-prediction loss differs from the supplement's L1 configuration. Equation 18 also gives a nonstandard PSNR numerator without the usual squared peak value. These may be reporting errors, but the implemented definitions and whether metrics evaluate individual samples or their mean should be stated.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, the paper makes a worthwhile computational-imaging contribution: reconstructing 31 spectral channels from a single filterless measurement using a diffractive optic. Combining a conditional patch diffusion prior with global measurement consistency and per-patch scale recovery provides a coherent solution to ambiguities caused by optical mixing across patch boundaries.

The principal simulated results are convincing within the tested setting. On ARAD1K, Table 1 reports 34.63 dB PSNR versus 31.77 dB for the strongest comparison, alongside improvements in SAM from 0.15 to 0.11 and SSIM from 0.90 to 0.94. Eight existing reconstruction methods are retrained for the proposed measurement model.

The ablations substantiate several design decisions. Table 2 demonstrates benefits from guidance and scale recovery, especially for small patches. Table 3 includes an achromatic control and multiple optical designs, providing evidence that chromatic encoding contributes beyond the learned image prior.

The evaluation extends beyond the primary benchmark through high-resolution cross-dataset examples, runtime–accuracy measurements, and supplementary experiments with noisy measurements. The uncertainty–error correlation is encouraging as an initial reliability indicator. The manuscript also supplies useful architecture and optical-simulation details.
weaknesses: The physical-camera claims exceed the validation. All measurements are simulated using a known, shift-invariant PSF; there is no captured-data experiment or assessment of PSF calibration errors, field-dependent aberrations, or fabrication mismatch. The supplementary Gaussian-noise study is useful but does not resolve these issues. A simulation-only algorithmic contribution can be valuable, but the conclusions about practical high-resolution, light-efficient cameras should be qualified.

The comparisons do not isolate the claimed advantage of patch-based learning. The proposed 75M-parameter diffusion model receives iterative physics guidance, whereas the comparison methods differ in architecture, training procedure, and inference computation. A matched full-image diffusion model and a comparable deterministic patch model with measurement-consistency refinement would help establish whether patching itself is responsible for the gains. The current results support superiority of the complete pipeline, but not the stronger conclusion that local processing is intrinsically more effective than larger receptive fields.

Claims that local optical cues capture 'full spectral information' are too strong for this severely underdetermined inverse problem. The results demonstrate recovery using learned natural-scene priors, not general spectral identifiability. Spatially uniform regions, unusual spectra, and narrow spectral features would be informative stress tests. Cross-dataset testing is limited to 10 scenes each from ICVL and Harvard and five CAVE scenes, without a stated selection protocol, comparative baselines, or aggregate spectral-angle results.

The RGB experiments are misleadingly labeled as Bayer measurements. Supplementary Section 11 clarifies that the reported results use three full-resolution filtered channels, effectively assuming sequential captures, rather than a single Bayer mosaic. This materially changes the measurement budget and acquisition setting. These columns should be relabeled, and the claimed small degradation with actual mosaics should be quantified.

The 'any resolution' claim is demonstrated more clearly for applicability than for practical scaling. Supplementary Table 4 gives approximately 21.82 seconds per 256 × 256 reconstruction under the default configuration, and uncertainty requires 10 reconstructions. High-resolution runtime and peak memory are not reported. The complexity discussion also does not explain how the coupled least-squares scale solve is implemented as the patch count increases.

Several reporting details limit reproducibility and interpretation: the main text specifies squared-error diffusion training while Table 5 specifies L1; Algorithm 1 omits the gradient normalization in Eq. (6); and the guidance step size is unspecified. The PSNR formula in Eq. (18) also needs clarification because its peak term is unsquared and depends on the prediction. Finally, correlation between sample variance and error supports an uncertainty heuristic, but does not establish calibrated predictive intervals or reliable detection of confidently incorrect spectra.

strengths: The paper addresses a compelling computational-imaging problem: reconstructing 31 spectral bands from a single grayscale measurement using one diffractive optic without increasing sensor pixel count. As an Algorithms/General contribution, the combination of patch-conditioned diffusion, global optical consistency, and patch-scale estimation provides a useful approach to a severely underdetermined inverse problem.

The main simulated results are strong. On ARAD1K, Table 1 reports 34.63 dB PSNR versus 31.77 dB for the strongest baseline, alongside improvements in SAM from 0.15 to 0.11 and SSIM from 0.90 to 0.94. Comparisons include eight reconstruction methods retrained for the proposed measurement model.

The ablations substantiate the central design choices. Table 2 demonstrates meaningful benefits from guidance and scale estimation, particularly for 32-pixel patches. The optical-design comparison also offers useful evidence about the trade-off between spectral mixing and spatial detail.

High-resolution reconstructions on ICVL and Harvard demonstrate practical flexibility beyond the training resolution. Supplementary noise experiments and the reported association between sample variance and reconstruction error broaden the evaluation beyond noiseless, in-distribution reconstruction.

The manuscript explains the pipeline clearly and provides substantial implementation and optical-design details. Overall, the demonstrated algorithmic gains support a slight preference for acceptance, although the broader physical and generalization claims need qualification.
weaknesses: The claim that local optical cues capture 'full spectral information' exceeds the evidence. Equation (1) remains highly underdetermined: for a spatially uniform scene away from boundaries, the measurement supplies only one weighted spectral integral. Successful reconstruction therefore depends critically on learned scene priors. The achromatic baseline and saliency analysis demonstrate that optical coding helps, but do not establish spectral identifiability. Controlled tests with ambiguous spectra or unfamiliar materials would better distinguish measurement-derived information from prior-driven inference.

The comparisons do not isolate the claimed advantage of patch-based learning over full-field reconstruction. There is no matched full-field diffusion model, or deterministic patch model with comparable normalization and measurement-consistency refinement. Architecture, capacity, inference computation, and patching change together across the principal comparisons. The results establish an effective overall system, but provide weaker support for the specific explanation that concentrating model capacity on local cues is superior.

Physical feasibility remains incompletely validated. All measurements use the assumed simulated forward model, and the noise study addresses additive Gaussian corruption rather than PSF calibration error, spatially varying aberrations, or depth variation. A fabricated camera is not essential for this algorithmic contribution, but sensitivity experiments are important to support the proposed high-resolution camera applications. The 32-pixel PSF support discussed in the main paper also needs reconciliation with the approximately 64-pixel physical support described in the supplement.

Generalization and uncertainty evidence is promising but limited. Cross-dataset averages cover only 10 scenes for ICVL and Harvard and five for CAVE, without a clear scene-selection protocol or baseline comparisons. The real/fake-object demonstration is qualitative. The reported uncertainty–error correlation does not establish calibrated predictive intervals or reliable detection of confidently incorrect spectra; Figure 7 also uses logarithmic axes, leaving the domain of the reported Pearson correlation unclear.

Several reporting details impede reproduction and interpretation. The guidance step size and scalable least-squares implementation are insufficiently specified, and Algorithm 1 omits the gradient normalization in Equation (6). High-resolution runtime and peak memory are missing despite scalability being central; Table 4 reports about 22 seconds per 256×256 reconstruction before repeated sampling. Supplement Section 11 also reveals that the 'Bayer' results use three full-resolution filtered channels rather than an actual mosaic. Finally, Equation (18) gives a nonstandard PSNR numerator, which should be corrected or reconciled with the evaluation code.

strengths: The paper presents a valuable computational-imaging contribution: reconstructing hyperspectral images from a single panchromatic measurement using a fabricated diffractive lens. The combination of optical simplicity, patch diffusion, and global measurement consistency is compelling even though its individual computational ingredients build on established methods.

Simulation results strongly support reconstruction quality in the proposed setting. On ARAD1K, the method achieves 34.63 dB PSNR versus 31.8 dB for the strongest reported baseline, with corresponding improvements in SAM and SSIM. Ablations substantiate the benefits of guidance, patch rescaling, and cross-patch coupling.

The physical prototype provides meaningful evidence beyond simulation: measured PSFs, spectral calibration, adaptation using six scenes, and evaluation on eight scenes with disjoint objects. The reported experimental averages of 31.20 dB PSNR and 0.157 SAM support feasibility under real optical and sensor mismatch.

The investigation is unusually broad, covering optical designs, measurement noise, cross-dataset reconstruction, CASSI, and resolution changes. The explicit homogeneous-region limitation and controlled checkerboard experiment help establish when the approach is informative and when spectral recovery becomes unreliable.

Sample variability provides a promising reliability indicator, supported by uncertainty–error correlations of 0.80 in simulation and 0.69 experimentally, per-channel analyses, and selective reconstruction results on CASSI.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not cleanly isolate the algorithmic contribution over existing patch-based inverse-problem diffusion methods. There is no directly adapted patch-diffusion baseline or matched full-image conditional diffusion baseline. The UNet regression comparison also changes both the learning objective and patch/full-image training, so it cannot establish which change explains the gains. This limits the strength of the claimed methodological advance, although the system-level contribution remains substantial.

Important sampling details are inconsistent or missing. The main text specifies an L2 noise-prediction objective, while Supplement Sec. S3.1 specifies L1. Equation (5) normalizes the guidance gradient, whereas Algorithm 1 does not; the algorithm also computes the noise prediction outside the inner guidance loop, leaving network reevaluation and differentiation unclear. The guidance step size, number of uncertainty samples, and whether reported reconstruction metrics use individual samples or their mean should be explicit. The simulation PSF support is also described as both 32 and 64 pixels, directly affecting the patch-size interpretation.

Real-data validation demonstrates feasibility more convincingly than comparative superiority. The experimental study lacks quantitative competing-method results under the same calibration and adaptation protocol, and the LoRA ablation is primarily qualitative. Approximate homography alignment also complicates interpretation of pixelwise spectral errors. Object-region metrics alongside full-crop averages would strengthen the evidence.

Uncertainty–error correlation supports relative reliability ranking but does not establish calibrated spectral uncertainty. Coverage tests, per-scene analyses, and checks controlling for intensity would clarify whether narrow sample spreads can conceal systematic errors, particularly in homogeneous regions and under distribution shift. The uncertainty envelopes should not be interpreted as validated confidence intervals.

Scalability is principally a capability to process larger images, not demonstrated computational efficiency: reconstruction rises from approximately 22 seconds at 256 × 256 to as much as 52 minutes on larger scenes, with experimental scenes taking 13 minutes. Memory measurements and a runtime breakdown including denoising, scale estimation, and guidance would better substantiate the complexity discussion. Distillation-based acceleration is proposed but not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper makes a meaningful computational-imaging contribution: reconstructing hyperspectral images from a single panchromatic measurement using one diffractive lens. Evaluated as Algorithms/General, its value lies in adapting patch diffusion to substantial optical mixing and demonstrating the resulting imaging system.

The main simulation results are strong: Table 1 reports 34.6 dB PSNR versus 31.8 dB for the strongest tested baseline, with improvements in both SAM and SSIM. Table 2 supports the importance of global guidance and patch rescaling through targeted ablations.

The fabricated metalens provides substantive physical validation beyond simulation. Eight held-out tabletop scenes achieve average PSNR of 31.20 dB and SAM of 0.157, with calibration, fabrication, and adaptation procedures described in the supplement.

Evaluation covers multiple optical designs, cross-dataset reconstruction, measurement noise, and an additional CASSI setting. The controlled homogeneous-region experiment and explicit discussion of reconstruction time provide useful evidence about practical limitations.

Sample variance provides a promising reliability indicator, with reported uncertainty–error correlations of 0.80 in simulation and 0.69 experimentally. Overall, the combined algorithmic and experimental evidence supports acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not fully isolate why the proposed method improves reconstruction. UNet-Regress changes both the learning objective and patch/full-image training, while there is no matched full-image diffusion or patch-regression baseline with comparable physical-consistency refinement. Direct comparison with the cited patch-diffusion inverse-problem approaches would better establish the methodological advance.

Important sampling details remain ambiguous. Equation (5) normalizes the guidance gradient, whereas supplementary Algorithm 1 does not; the algorithm computes the denoiser output outside the inner loop without clarifying whether it is recomputed or differentiated through after updates. The guidance step size, number of uncertainty samples, and whether quantitative results use individual samples or sample means should be specified. The main text's squared-error training objective also differs from the supplement's L1 objective.

Uncertainty–error correlation supports error ranking but does not establish calibrated posterior uncertainty. Coverage measurements and sensitivity to guidance strength would be valuable because strong guidance can reduce sample diversity without resolving spectral ambiguity. The claims should distinguish empirical reliability indicators from validated posterior samples.

Physical validation remains limited to eight indoor scenes, with approximate reference-image registration and no quantitative comparison against competing reconstruction methods on the real measurements. This supports feasibility more strongly than real-world superiority. Object-region metrics would also help interpret full-crop scores in scenes containing substantial background.

Some broader interpretations exceed the evidence. PSF-shaped saliency and selected metameric examples do not establish that learned scene statistics are unimportant. Similarly, the Bayer experiment uses fully sampled three-channel measurements and does not provide an equal-photon-budget demonstration of the proposed throughput advantage.

Reconstruction cost substantially limits deployment: approximately 13 minutes per experimental scene and up to 52 minutes for larger simulated scenes, before accounting for repeated uncertainty sampling. This acknowledged tradeoff is compatible with snapshot acquisition, but the practical scope is considerably narrower than the compact hardware alone suggests.

strengths: The paper makes a worthwhile computational-imaging contribution: recovering hyperspectral images from a single panchromatic measurement using a diffractive lens without a sensor color-filter array. Under the default Algorithms/General criteria, the combination of reconstruction methodology, optical investigation, and physical validation supports acceptance.

The integration of conditional patch diffusion, least-squares patch rescaling, and global optical guidance addresses a concrete difficulty: substantial signal crosses patch boundaries when PSF support approaches or exceeds patch size. Table 2 provides useful evidence that guidance and rescaling each contribute, and that overlapping patches alone do not recover the same performance.

Simulation results are strong across several metrics. On ARAD1K, the method achieves approximately 34.6 dB PSNR versus 31.8 dB for the strongest reported baseline, with corresponding improvements in SAM and SSIM. Cross-dataset tests, alternative optical designs, noise experiments, and supplementary CASSI results broaden the evidence beyond one configuration.

The fabricated metalens prototype substantially strengthens the feasibility case. Eight held-out tabletop scenes achieve average PSNR/SAM/SSIM of 31.20/0.157/0.894 after adaptation on six scenes without shared objects. The supplement describes fabrication, spectral calibration, alignment, and experimental PSF characterization in useful detail.

The uncertainty estimates offer practical value, with reported error correlations of 0.80 in simulation and 0.69 experimentally, supported by per-channel analysis. The paper also candidly analyzes homogeneous-region failures and supplies a controlled checkerboard experiment, helping delimit where the imaging approach is informative.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not fully isolate the source of improvement. The UNet regression control changes both the objective and the patch/full-image formulation. A matched patchwise regression model with the same normalization and optical-consistency refinement would better establish the specific benefit of diffusion. Comparisons with existing patch-based diffusion inverse-problem methods would also clarify novelty beyond combining established components.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistencies in the central algorithm description. Section 3.2 specifies squared-error noise prediction, whereas Supplement S3.1 specifies an L1 objective. Equation (5) normalizes the guidance gradient, but Algorithm 1 does not; the algorithm also leaves unclear whether noise predictions are recomputed inside the guidance loop. The guidance step size and number of samples used for uncertainty should be explicitly reported. The claimed PSF width is also inconsistent between Sections 4.3 and 5.1.

The physical results establish a promising proof of concept, but comparative evidence is confined largely to simulation. The real experiment lacks quantitatively evaluated competing reconstruction methods under matched adaptation, and approximate homography registration complicates interpretation of pixelwise reference metrics. Eight indoor scenes and a central crop provide limited evidence about broader deployment conditions.

Uncertainty–error correlation establishes a useful ranking signal, not calibrated posterior uncertainty. Coverage measurements, sample-count sensitivity, and evaluation of confidently incorrect predictions under distribution shift would strengthen this claim. The plotted sample ranges should not be interpreted as confidence intervals without further validation.

Practical scalability remains limited: reconstruction takes about 13 minutes for experimental crops and up to 52 minutes for high-resolution scenes on an RTX 3090. Repeated sampling adds further cost. The demonstrated throughput/accuracy trade-off is therefore narrower than the compact optical hardware might suggest; an exposure- and noise-matched comparison would also be needed to quantify the proposed light-throughput advantage.
